notes:
I've written notes for every verse except v. 17, where my only source was the Catholic Haydock commentary (it's under "Other views"). A few gaps first:

- **Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org) and Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com):** none of my searches turned up their material on this chapter.
- **Prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace:** I found no material on this chapter, so that section is missing.
- **Modern scholarship:** I didn't reach the netbible.org notes. The only scholarly source is one Bible Odyssey article.
- **Tradition labels:** these come only from the pages themselves or from your list of sites. StudyLight tags Gill as "Baptist · Calvinism"; Haydock is the Catholic commentary.
- **Haydock links:** the Haydock page was fetched rather than searched, so I give its URL without the quote tags used elsewhere.

**v. 1**
- Gill: Ahab described the miracles at Carmel. The people were now on Elijah's side, so Ahab could not seize him. this he said to clear himself, and make her easy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-1.html
- Gill: "all the prophets" means the 450 prophets of Baal. The 400 prophets of the grove weren't at Carmel; Jezebel knew they were safe, being with her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html
- Matthew Henry: Ahab's conscience held him back from persecuting Elijah himself, so he stirred up Jezebel. That queen-consort, it seems, was in effect queen-regent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Jezebel did not admit Baal had been proven false. She vowed to kill Elijah within a day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
- Was the threat real? Henry thinks she didn't dare touch him for fear of the people, all counting him a prophet, so she sent the message only to frighten him away. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm
- Guzik quotes Patterson and Austel: had she really wanted him dead, she would have seized him without warning. Her aim was to discredit Elijah and his God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/

**v. 3**
- Gill: the hero of Carmel is now frightened by one woman. This shows his courage were of the Lord, and not of himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html
- Was the flight God's will? Opinions differ:
  - Guzik is unsure. We cannot say for certain if this was led of God or not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
  - Precept Austin notes the text doesn't say God told him to run or that he prayed first. His actions strongly suggest he is out of the will of the LORD. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-19-commentary
  - Haydock (Catholic), citing Theodoret: God let Elijah flee so that he would learn humility. Haydock calls the idea that Elijah had a hidden fault groundless. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): Elijah failed in the very point at which he was strongest, and that is where most men fail. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: by "It is enough" Elijah meant he couldn't go on. Carmel brought no lasting national revival. Elijah forgot that people reject God *despite* the evidence, not *because* of the evidence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
- Guzik: God said no to this prayer, and Elijah never died at all. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
- **Where interpreters differ:**
  - Gill (Baptist): the wish was not like Paul's longing to be with Christ but like that of Job and of Jonah, a wish to escape trouble. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html
  - Henry agrees: it was the passionate wish of his corruption, as Job's. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm
  - Haydock/Challoner (Catholic) disagrees: Elijah asked to die out of zeal against sin, not impatience or cowardice. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html
- Gill's geography: this was the wilderness of Paran, about 20 miles south of Beersheba. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html

**v. 5**
- Gill: far from granting his request, God made provision to preserve it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html
- Guzik: God met Elijah's bodily needs first. Sometimes the most *spiritual* thing a person can do is get enough rest and replenishment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/

**v. 6**
- Gill: the bread may have been "baked on hot stones," which an angel could have heated. He also notes one view that the water jar was Elijah's own. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-6.html
- Guzik: one nap and one meal were not enough. He also quotes Spurgeon that food and rest may be the first help a depressed servant of God needs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/

**v. 7**
- Gill: there would be no ordinary food on the road, hence the second meal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: like a wise doctor, God gave food, rest and exercise before reasoning with him, because before, Elijah's mind was unfit for reasoning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-9.html

**v. 8**
- **Forty days:**
  - Gill: the trip could have taken three or four days. Elijah wandered, as Israel did for forty years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html
  - Constable: the walk takes about 14 days. Elijah was getting the same discipline for weak faith that Israel had received. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/1-kings-19.html
  - Ligonier (Reformed) points to Israel's desert food and Moses' forty days on Sinai. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/elijah-at-horeb
- Henry: God showed that man does not live by bread alone. Henry also says Thither the Spirit of the Lord led him, probably beyond his own intention. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm
- **Catholic:** Challoner (in Haydock) sees this bread as a picture of the Eucharist, which sustains believers on their journey to God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html

**v. 9**
- The cave: Guzik quotes Wiseman that it may be the same "cleft of the rock" where God appeared to Moses (Exod. 33:22). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
  - Gill says Jewish writers held this view but doubts it, since Elijah was told to go out of the cave. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-9.html
- **"What are you doing here?"**
  - Gill: it is a mild rebuke. A prophet could do no service in a cave. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-9.html
  - Constable: God hadn't sent him to Horeb; Elijah had fled to Horeb out of fear. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/1-kings-19.html
  - Precept Austin compares God's question "Where are you?" in Genesis 3:9; the question is for Elijah's benefit, not God's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-19-commentary

**v. 10**
- Keil (on Bible Hub): Elijah's "very zealous" echoes Phinehas. But whereas Phinehas received the promise of an everlasting priesthood for his zeal, Elijah had seen so little fruit. The same page reads the complaint as a quiet appeal for God to judge Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/19-10.htm
  - Gill reads it the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html
- Henry: the torn-down altars were private altars used by faithful people who couldn't go to Jerusalem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm
- "I alone": Guzik says it was not accurate, but it is how he felt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
  - Haydock (Catholic) adds that in Judah true religion was then flourishing. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html
- Vance Havner (Baptist preacher; quoted on Precept Austin) calls him the surviving saint, with a martyr complex. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-19-commentary

**v. 11**
- Constable: God repeated the displays of power from Sinai and Carmel. God wasn't "in" them in the sense that they were not His methods now. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/1-kings-19.html
- Henry: Moses was put into the cave when God passed by, but Elijah was called out of it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm
- Gill notes that the Targum and Rashi took the wind, earthquake and fire to be hosts of angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-12.html

**v. 12** (the most debated verse)
- **Translation:** the NRSV has "a sound of sheer silence"; the ESV footnote has Or a sound, a thin silence. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/19-12.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/esv/1ki/19/9/s_310009
  - Barnes: literally "a sound of soft stillness." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/1-kings/19-12.html
- **Common evangelical reading:** quiet words to the heart achieve more than displays of power. Guzik: displays of power* and *preaching God's anger* don't necessarily change hearts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
  - Spurgeon (Baptist): He does use the wind, the earthquake and the fire when He pleases, but these are not His most effective instruments. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons55/sermons55.xlvii.html
- **Law versus gospel:**
  - Gill (Baptist/Calvinist) reads the scene as the difference between law and gospel. The law came amid storm and quake; the gospel is a gentle voice of grace. It also mirrors how God first breaks hearts by the law, then speaks peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-12.html
  - Henry sees the gospel's gentler voice here too. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-10.html
- **A rebuke of Elijah's zeal?** Barnes: The teaching is a condemnation of that "zeal" which Elijah had gloried in. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-12.html
- **Do the storm and fire still have a place?** Havner says God does speak in wind (Pentecost), earthquake (the cross and resurrection) and fire (the tongues of fire), but also in a whisper. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-19-commentary
  - Hastings: these displays get people ready to hear God's voice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hastings/1_kings/19-11.htm
- **Hearing God inwardly:** Chuck Smith (in StudyLight's commentaries) applies the verse to God's inner voice. It can feel So natural that it seems like it comes maybe even from your own heart or your own mind, yet it is God speaking. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-10.html
- **Pentecostal (ag.org):** an Assemblies of God article stresses silence itself as a sign of God's presence. For this verse, silence is central. https://news.ag.org/en/articles/news/2020/07/the%20sounds%20of%20silence
- **Catholic (Haydock):**
  - Citing Grotius: God showed the difference between the law's terror and the gospel's mildness.
  - Citing others: Elijah was to moderate his zeal and win sinners by gentle means.
  - https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html
- **Orthodox (OCA):** Metropolitan Tikhon applies it to the Church today. When society turns from Christ, the Church should not answer through tempestuous outrage, earth-quaking tirades, or emotionally-fired speech, nor give in to self-pity. https://www.oca.org/reflections/metropolitan-tikhon/the-still-small-voice-of-god
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey):**
  - It finds Elijah's claim to be the only faithful one ironic, given how Carmel turned out.
  - The "sound of sheer silence" reassures him that he is not alone.
  - https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/elijah/

**v. 13**
- Henry: storm, quake and fire didn't make Elijah cover his face, but the quiet voice did. Gracious souls are more affected by the tender mercies of the Lord than by his terrors. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm
- Why did he cover his face?
  - Gill: out of reverence and shame, like the seraphim (Isa. 6) and Moses. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html
  - Constable: he knew he couldn't look at God and live. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-19.html
- Pulpit Commentary: the gentle voice seems to be what first got him to obey the order to go out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-13.html
- Spurgeon: God named him personally. It is a mark of God's Spirit that when he speaks to men he speaks to them personally. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-12.html

**v. 14**
- Constable: Elijah evidently understood the lesson but he still felt depressed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-14.html
- Chuck Smith: Elijah still didn't understand the question and gave the same answer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-10.html
- Gill: God drew out the repeated complaint so he could explain how judgment would come, through the kings and the prophet Elijah would anoint. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-19.html

**v. 15**
- Guzik: God gave Elijah something to do, so he would stop dwelling on himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
- Havner: God didn't demote the tired prophet; he told him to pass the torch on. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-19-commentary
- Haydock (Catholic): Elijah doesn't seem to have anointed Hazael in person. It was done through Elisha (2 Kings 8), and "anoint" may simply mean "declare king." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html

**v. 16**
- Guzik: Elisha was a friend as well as a successor, the answer to Elijah's complaint that he was alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-19/
- Haydock (Catholic): Jehu was actually anointed by one of Elisha's disciples (2 Kings 9). The Church Fathers inferred from this verse that prophets were anointed too. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html

**v. 18**
- Precept Austin: the seven thousand correct Elijah's mistaken belief that he was alone. Some scholars view seven thousand as symbolizing fullness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-19-commentary
- Gill: "kissed him" means kissing Baal's image, or kissing one's hand toward it. The verb may be "I have left" (now) or "I will reserve" (later). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-18.html
- **The remnant, in different traditions:**
  - Henry: only God's grace preserves them, a remnant according to the election of grace (Rom. 11). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm
  - Ligonier (Reformed): God keeps a remnant in every generation through the ordinary means of His Word and through the decisions of human agents. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/elijah-at-horeb
  - Precept Austin: this begins the Bible's "remnant" theme, which leads on to the New Testament church. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-19-commentary
  - Haydock (Catholic) draws a different lesson: the true Church was never in danger of perishing entirely. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html
- Spurgeon: the seven thousand show that Elijah's everyday life had borne fruit. The still small voice had been doing for Israel what Elijah could not do! https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons55/sermons55.xlvii.html

**v. 19**
- Twelve teams of oxen: Gill reports Kimchi's view that this signified Elisha would lead the twelve tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-19.html
  - Constable suggests the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-19.html
- Barnes: putting the cloak on him was a kind of adoption, as a father clothes his children. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-19.html
- Henry: Elisha didn't seek Elijah; the call came first. We love God, and choose him, because he chose us, and loved us, first. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm

**v. 20**
- Constable: "What have I done to you?" is an idiom meaning "do as you please." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-19.html
- Henry: Elijah won't force him; let him count the cost. The efficacy of God's grace preserves the native liberty of man's will. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_019.cfm
- Haydock (Catholic) links the verse to Luke 9:62 (looking back from the plough). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html

**v. 21**
- Constable: killing the oxen as a sacrifice symbolized his total personal commitment to God. He also quotes Auld: Elijah recruits his successor at work, as Jesus would with his followers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-19.html
- Gill: the feast showed Elisha's joy at being called. As Elijah's servant he was trained for the prophet's office. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/19-21.html
- Haydock (Catholic): the oxen show that he gave up his old trade; Jerome says he "makes a vow of them." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-kings-19.html
